prompt.context: Your friend, a current MBA student, has his heart set on starting a barbershop in Evanston after graduation. There are plenty of barbershops and salons near the Northwestern campus, but your eager friend argues they are either (A) vastly overpriced or (B) cheap, but really low quality. He wants your help coming up with a plan.
prompt.question: Develop a market entry strategy for Busch's Barber Shop in Evanston. Help your friend decide whether and how to enter this market.

clarifying_info.a: For this analysis, your friend wants to focus solely on the male population of Evanston.

clarifying_info.q: What is the competitive landscape like?
clarifying_info.a: Highly competitive, segmented into two distinct groups: high price & low quality. Your friend believes there is a profitable space in between these two segments.
Growing at GDP the past five years.

clarifying_info.q: What is your friend's background and financial situation?
clarifying_info.a: No specific experience in cosmetology; has enough savings to fund initial upfront costs and early ongoing costs.
Profitability is the main goal in the short term — wants to be profitable in year one to justify his decision not to take a high-paying consulting job.

clarifying_info.q: What services will the barbershop offer?
clarifying_info.a: The barbershop initially intends to sell haircut service only. Any other additional products or services can be considered in the future.

exhibits.title: Market Analysis
exhibits.shows: Pie chart showing where men in Evanston get their haircut (split between low-end $ at 67% and high-end $$$ at 33%), plus a stacked bar chart showing competitors' market share within each segment. Notes indicate the market is split between two groups.

exhibits.title: Market Entry Projections
exhibits.shows: Table comparing two potential locations (Downtown and Not Downtown) across expected customer steal percentages from low-end and high-end segments, upfront costs (equipment and advertising), and ongoing costs (rent and labor).

data.note: Customer steal projections based on consumer survey describing new barbershop as in-between quality at price point of $30.

framework: Client: Goals (year-one profitability), strengths/resources (savings cover upfront + early ongoing costs), no cosmetology experience
Market: Size and growth (GDP growth), competition (two segments — high price/quality vs low price/quality), customer segmentation (adult male population of Evanston)
Profitability: Expected customer volume (market steal from each segment), pricing ($30 mid-tier), revenue, fixed costs (equipment, advertising, rent), variable costs (hourly labor)
Go-to-market strategy: Build new shop (vs acquire or partner), location choice (downtown vs not downtown), marketing and customer acquisition
Barriers: Capital requirements, local regulations, attracting qualified barber talent
Risks: Competitive response from incumbents, insufficient differentiation, opportunity cost of capital and foregone salary

questions.prompt: Estimate the size of the adult men's haircut market in Evanston.
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure the sizing with explicit assumptions: Evanston adult population (~60k), male/female split (~50/50 = 30k males), adjust for men who actually pay for haircuts (exclude young kids, bald men, those who cut their own hair — roughly 80% = 24k paying men), factor in % who get cuts in Evanston vs elsewhere (~80% = ~19k), average haircuts per year (~10), and price split between low-end ($20, 67%) and high-end ($50, 33%). Candidate should produce a total annual spend figure. Push for speed — this is not the primary focus.

math.setup: Estimate annual dollar market using population, segmentation, frequency, and price.
math.answer: Approximately $9M annual market for men's haircuts in Evanston

questions.prompt: Calculate projected first-year revenue and costs for each of the two locations, and determine which is more profitable.
questions.guidance: Candidate should use Exhibit A to find adult male counts per segment and Exhibit B to apply steal percentages. Revenue = customers stolen * 10 cuts/year * $30/cut. Costs = upfront (equipment + advertising) + ongoing (rent annual + labor annual). Labor = workers * $15/hr * 10 hr/day * 360 days. Compare profit = revenue minus total cost for each location.

math.setup: Revenue and cost comparison for Downtown vs Not Downtown locations.
math.answer: Downtown location yields ~$436k first-year profit vs ~$275k for Not Downtown. Downtown is the better choice.

questions.prompt: Your friend (having chosen the downtown location) wants to implement a loyalty program giving customers their 10th haircut free. He projects this will increase total first-year customers by 10%. Is this a profitable decision?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate new revenue under the loyalty program. With 10 haircuts per year and every 10th free, each customer pays for only 9 haircuts annually. New customer count = 2,500 * 110% = 2,750. New revenue = 2,750 * 9 * $30. Compare to prior revenue of $750k. Costs remain constant (employees paid hourly; assume no additional employees needed).

math.setup: Compare revenue with vs without loyalty program, holding costs constant.
steps: Paid haircuts per customer per year: 10 - 1 (free 10th) = 9
math.answer: Revenue decreases by ~$7,500 (~1%). Since costs are unchanged, the loyalty program is not profitable at current growth projections.

brainstorming.prompt: What other factors should be considered when choosing a potential shop location? What changes could make the loyalty program profitable? What are pros and cons of a membership-based pricing model? How would you attract and retain quality barber talent without paying the high base wages of high-end competitors?

categories.name: Location factors
ideas: Proximity to complementary stores (e.g., gyms, coffee shops)
Store layout and capacity for future barber chairs
Preference and accessibility for target demographic (Northwestern students, professionals)

categories.name: Loyalty program adjustments
ideas: Decrease frequency of freebies (e.g., every 15th cut free instead of 10th)
Offer a discount (50% off) rather than a fully free cut
Tiered rewards with upsell opportunities (e.g., free product with 10th cut)
Implement only for year one to build initial customer base, then evaluate

categories.name: Membership pricing model
ideas: Pros: More predictable recurring revenue stream; increased customer data; differentiation from competitors
Cons: Adverse selection — only high-frequency users will subscribe; potential tip reduction frustrating employees; capacity constraints if too many unlimited members

categories.name: Talent attraction & retention
ideas: More flexible work schedules than high-end competitors
End-of-year profit sharing to align employee interests with shop success
Target rising stars currently working in low-end shops who want advancement
Invest in training to build loyalty among newer talent
Competitive tip environment given mid-tier positioning

recommendation: Your friend should open the downtown location without implementing the loyalty program as proposed.
Projected first-year profit at the downtown location is approximately $436k, significantly exceeding the not-downtown option (~$275k).
The loyalty program in its current form (free 10th cut) reduces revenue by ~$7,500 with no cost savings, making it unprofitable.
risks: Customer acquisition projections assume immediate steal from existing shops — in reality, ramp-up time means year-one revenue could be materially lower without an effective marketing campaign.
Competitive response: high-end shops may discount if they lose customers, though projected steal from high-end is only 5% — unlikely to trigger drastic retaliation.
Customers may not perceive sufficient quality improvement over low-end options to justify the $30 price point (vs $20), reducing actual steal rates.
Opportunity cost: the friend is forgoing a high-paying consulting job and deploying all personal savings — downside scenarios must be stress-tested.
next_steps: Perform due diligence on potentially acquiring an existing Evanston barbershop rather than building from scratch.
Conduct more extensive customer surveys to validate steal projections and price sensitivity at $30.
Research how to hire and retain qualified barbers who can deliver quality meaningfully above low-end competitors.
Sign lease, purchase equipment, bring on an experienced cosmetology advisor, and develop a formal marketing strategy.
Re-evaluate the loyalty program structure (e.g., lower freebie frequency, discount instead of free) to identify a profitable version.
